22925-the-story-of-young-abraham-lincoln:
Wayne Whipple tells The Story of Young Abraham Lincoln for young readers. With all his brain and brawn, Whipple writes, Lincoln's real greatness lay in his heart. Whipple calls him the great-hearted man of the White House. Far more people know Lincoln's name, he adds, than ever met Bunyan's Great-Heart on the page.

The biography follows Lincoln from log-cabin childhood toward the presidency, stressing kindness, honesty, and hard study. Whipple shapes true events into episodes a child can hold, the rail fence, the borrowed book, the wrestling match. Such lives of Lincoln filled schoolrooms for decades. This one keeps the period's reverent tone, and its Bunyan comparison shows how Americans framed their hero.
abraham-lincoln:
James Russell Lowell writes on Abraham Lincoln while the Civil War still rages and Lincoln still sits in the White House. Lowell, a poet and critic, sizes up a president many in the East had dismissed as a rough westerner. The essay argues that Lincoln's plain sense, patience, and honesty fit the crisis exactly.

He weighs Lincoln's speeches and acts, his handling of generals and factions, and his slow movement on slavery. Lowell's prose is careful and warm, rising at the close to real eloquence. Coming from a leading man of letters, the piece helped fix Lincoln's standing with educated readers who had doubted him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-eins:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Einsiedeln describes a Benedictine monastery in Schwyz, Switzerland, named for Our Lady of the Hermits. The place takes its name from its hermit founders. St. Meinrad, educated at Reichenau, embraced the hermit's life on Mount Etzel with a wonder-working statue of Our Lady given by Abbess Hildegard of Zurich.

Robbers murdered Meinrad in 861 for the shrine's treasures, yet hermits kept his place for eighty years. Then Eberhard, former provost of Strasburg, built a monastery and church and became its first abbot. Legend says the church gained a miraculous consecration, and pilgrims have crowded Einsiedeln ever since. The entry follows the shrine from hermitage to great abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-chris:
Blessed Christine of Stommeln, a mystic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Stommeln near Cologne in 1242 to a well-to-do peasant, Heinrich Bruso, she died in 1312. At five she saw visions of the Christ Child, her mystic spouse from age ten, and at eleven she learned to read the Psalter, though she could not write.

When her parents sought a marriage for her at twelve, she fled to the Beguines at Cologne, a community of devout women, and lived a life of severe penance. Visions, stigmata, and demonic torments fill her later story, recorded by her Dominican confessor. The entry presents a peasant girl of extraordinary inner life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-hugh-of: St. Hugh of Lincoln was the Carthusian bishop. This entry traces his Witham, his Lincoln, and his sanctity. The swan's bishop: his tame swan guarded the saint at Stow in Lincolnshire's fens in the 1100s' decades of the Norman kings.
quotes-and-images-from-the-writings-of-a:
Quotes and Images from Abraham Lincoln, prepared by David Widger, gathers quotations and subject references from the eight volumes of The Writings of Abraham Lincoln. Widger's note sets the span. It runs from Lincoln's first political address in 1832. It ends with a hastily scrawled note on the day of his assassination. Steel engravings and photographs are included. They are meant to give the words greater impact.

The extracts open in war: a hundred thousand former slaves now serve in the United States military, slavery is abolished in Washington, and "the war came." Lincoln's rule stands here in his own words: as he would not be a slave, so he would not be a master.
the-boys-life-of-abraham-lincoln:
Helen Nicolay wrote The Boys' Life of Abraham Lincoln. The first part, A President's Childhood, traces his stock. His forefathers were pioneers who left home to open the wilds for those who came after. The first of them reached Massachusetts from England in 1638. For one hundred and seventy years since, the line had moved slow west.

Kentucky was his birthplace, on February 12, 1809. There his parents lived in deep want, in a rude log cabin. Nicolay calls Lincoln a pioneer of a nobler sort, one who led men's thoughts toward the right. His tale starts and ends in blood. His grandfather Abraham was shot by an Indian while at work with his three sons on their clearing. Mordecai, the eldest, shot the Indian who stooped to seize small Thomas, age six, and held the cabin till help came from the fort.
the-life-of-abraham-lincoln: Henry Ketcham wrote his life of Abraham Lincoln and dedicated it to two older brothers who served under Lincoln in the Civil War. Only the title page, dedication, and contents are present here. Chapters run from the wild West and the Lincoln family through Indiana years. Law practice, slavery debates, the nomination of 1860, Fort Sumter, and emancipation follow in the list. The biography itself does not appear here beyond those chapter titles.
the-southerner-a-romance-of-the-real-lin: Thomas Dixon subtitled this novel a romance of the real Lincoln, publishing it with D. Appleton and Company in New York and London in 1913, with illustrations by J. N. Marchand. The pages present here are front matter only. A Walt Whitman remark calls Lincoln essentially a Southern contribution. A dedication honours Woodrow Wilson as the first Southern-born president since Lincoln and Dixon's friend and collegemate. A list of Dixon's other novels includes The Leopard's Spots and The Clansman, so the story itself does not appear.
